Last updated November 14, 2026.

What the official sources say

  • Appeals of an assessment on the subsequent property roll are due the fourth Monday of November; missed-roll appeals are due before the board adjourns at its January meeting. (Idaho Code 63-501A; source)
  • The board of equalization may consider an appeal only if it is timely filed. (Idaho Code 63-501A; source)
  • A decision of the county board of equalization may be appealed to the Board of Tax Appeals within 30 days after mailing of notice of the decision or pronouncement at hearing; the same appeal may alternatively be taken to district court in that period. (Idaho Code 63-511. Appeals from county board of equalization; source)
  • Filing an appeal does not suspend payment of property taxes pending the appeal. (Idaho Code 63-511; source)
  • The notice of appeal to the BTA is filed with the clerk/auditor of the county where the property is located; the BTA has no filing fee. (File an Appeal | Idaho Board of Tax Appeals; source)
  • Before the tax deed issues, notice of pending issue must be sent by certified mail to record owners and parties in interest no more than five months nor less than two months before the deed issues, and an affidavit of compliance recorded. (Idaho Code 63-1005(1)-(2); source)
Selling in Idaho?

Get My Cash Offer →

When is Idaho property tax due, and can it be paid in halves?

Idaho property tax is due in full on or before December 20 of the year the tax is levied, and owners may instead pay in two halves. The first half is due by December 20, and a grace period runs to June 20 for the second half as long as the first half is paid in full (Idaho Code 63-903).

Any part of the tax can be paid at any time, but early payment does not erase costs, interest or late charges that have already accrued. If the first half is not fully paid by December 20, late charges and interest are assessed on whatever remains of that half. The same rule applies to the second half after June 20.

Taxes on a subsequent or missed roll follow a different clock. The tax collector must bill those within 30 days after the roll is delivered, and the deadline to pay is the same June 20 date. If the tax is still unpaid after June 20, it is delinquent. A seller who finds a second, unexpected bill on a parcel should ask the county treasurer whether it belongs to a missed roll.

What date does Idaho use to value a house for tax?

Idaho values taxable property as of 12:01 a.m. on January 1 of the year the tax is levied. Real, personal and operating property are all assessed annually at market value for assessment purposes as of that moment (Idaho Code 63-205).

That January 1 date matters when you sell. A house that sells in October has still been valued as it stood the previous January 1, so repairs or damage after that date do not change the value on the current bill. If a house burned or was gutted in the spring and the roll still reflects the old condition, the place to raise it is the county assessor, and the appeal windows described elsewhere on this page are strict.

Idaho keeps the assessor (who sets value) separate from the treasurer (who bills and collects). Calls about value go to the first office. Calls about balances, payoff figures and payment history go to the second.

What does a late payment cost in Idaho?

Interest on a delinquency is charged at one percent per month, calculated from January 1 following the year the tax lien attached. Interest is not charged on collection costs (Idaho Code 63-1001). On top of interest, late charges apply under section 63-201.

The money collected is passed to the county auditor, who divides late charges and interest among the taxing districts in the same proportion each district receives in tax. Paying current taxes does not stop a delinquency proceeding that is already under way for an earlier year (Idaho Code 63-903(7)).

A short worked example helps with planning. A balance left unpaid after the December 20 deadline begins to carry interest from the following January 1. Because the rate is monthly, a year of delay adds twelve months of interest to the unpaid amount before late charges and costs are counted. Ask the treasurer for an exact payoff figure for the day you plan to close, because the number moves every month.

Idaho property tax dates at a glance

This table pulls the main Idaho dates into one place. County offices can add local rules, so confirm with your treasurer and assessor.

EventDate or ruleSource
Valuation date12:01 a.m., January 1 of the levy yearIdaho Code 63-205
Tax due in full, or first halfDecember 20Idaho Code 63-903
Second half dueJune 20 of the following yearIdaho Code 63-903
Interest on delinquency1% per month from January 1 after the lien attachesIdaho Code 63-1001
Property Tax Reduction application (2027 taxes)January 1 to April 15, 2027Idaho State Tax Commission
Property Tax Deferral application (2027 taxes)January 1 to September 7, 2027Idaho State Tax Commission
Tax deed to the countyNot redeemed within 3 years of delinquencyIdaho Code 63-1005

Which Idaho programs can lower or delay a home's property tax?

Idaho has three homeowner programs run by the State Tax Commission and the county assessors, and each one needs an application. They sit alongside the homestead exemption, which is covered on its own page.

  • Property Tax Reduction. It could cut taxes by $250 to $1,500 on a home and up to one acre. For 2027, total 2026 income after medical expenses must be $40,030 or less, and the applicant must be 65 or older, blind, widowed, disabled, a former POW or hostage, or a fatherless or motherless child under 18. You apply every year between January 1 and April 15, and an approved benefit shows on the December bill (Tax Commission).
  • Property Tax Deferral. It postpones the tax on a home and up to one acre, but you must pay the tax and interest later. For 2027 the income limit is $63,400, and applications run from January 1 to September 7. The state pays the county directly, so the deferral does not appear on your bill (Tax Commission).
  • Disabled Veterans benefit. It can reduce tax by as much as $1,500 for a veteran with a 100% service-connected disability, with no income limit. The application window is also January 1 to April 15 (Tax Commission).

None of these programs reduces solid waste, irrigation or other fees that local governments charge. Because deferral creates a debt that has to be repaid, a seller who used it should ask the assessor how that balance is handled before the house closes.

What happens if an Idaho owner stops paying for years?

If delinquent real property is not redeemed within three years of the delinquency date, the county tax collector must make a tax deed to the county (Idaho Code 63-1005). The county cannot take the deed until it has given notice of the pending issue and recorded an affidavit of compliance.

The notice rules are specific:

  • Notice goes to the record owners and parties in interest by certified mail with return receipt, no more than five months and no less than two months before the deed is set to issue.
  • Publication must run at least once a week for four consecutive weeks, with the last notice at least 14 days before the deed date.
  • The notice must name the owner, describe the parcel, give the year of the delinquency, itemize what is owed, and say when and where the deed will issue.
  • The tax collector signs an affidavit of compliance at least five working days before issuance, and it is recorded with the county recorder.

Record owners also pay the costs of preparing, serving and publishing the notice, and those costs become a perpetual lien in favor of the tax collector. Even after a tax deed issues, the record owner or a party in interest may still redeem until the county commissioners enter into a contract of sale (Idaho Code 63-1007).

How do you sell an Idaho house that still has tax due?

You can sell a house with unpaid Idaho property tax, because the balance is normally settled out of the sale proceeds when the deal closes. The practical steps are short, and the order matters.

  1. Ask the county treasurer for a written payoff that lists each delinquent year, interest and costs, with a good-through date.
  2. Check whether any year is close to the three-year mark. A parcel that is nearing a tax deed has a hard deadline that sits above any closing date.
  3. Give the payoff figure to the title or escrow company so it can be paid from proceeds.
  4. Ask the assessor about any homestead exemption, deferral or reduction on the parcel before you transfer.

Counties explain the timing risk on their own sites. Kootenai County, for example, warns that escrow may not pay the treasurer when a closing happens before annual tax information is available or before the second installment is due, which can leave the buyer or seller holding the credit instead. Sellers in any county should ask the title company how current-year taxes will be prorated and who will actually send the payment.

The homestead statute adds one more point for owners. If a house is sold to a bona fide purchaser for value before a notice of intent to attach a lien for improperly claimed exemption is recorded, the assessor and treasurer stop recovering that unpaid amount (Idaho Code 63-602G). That protects the buyer, and it is a reason to correct any exemption problem before listing.

More questions about Idaho Property Tax Guide

When are Idaho property taxes due?

They are due in full by December 20, or in two halves with the first half due December 20 and the second half due June 20 of the next year, provided the first half is paid in full.

How much interest does Idaho charge on late property tax?

One percent per month, calculated from January 1 following the year the lien attached, plus late charges. Interest is not charged on collection costs.

Can I sell my Idaho house if I owe back property tax?

Yes. The unpaid tax, interest and costs are usually paid from closing proceeds, so get a written payoff from the county treasurer and give it to the title or escrow company.

Does Idaho have help for seniors or disabled homeowners with property tax?

Yes. The Property Tax Reduction program can lower tax by $250 to $1,500 for qualifying owners, the Disabled Veterans benefit can reduce it by up to $1,500, and Property Tax Deferral lets qualifying owners postpone tax, which must be repaid later with interest.

How long before a county can take a house for unpaid Idaho property tax?

If delinquent real property is not redeemed within three years of the delinquency date, the county tax collector must issue a tax deed to the county after proper notice and a recorded affidavit of compliance.

title: Idaho Homestead Exemption: Eligibility, Filing and Selling the Home
content:
Idaho Homestead Exemption: Eligibility, Filing and Selling the Home

Cash Home Buyers in Idaho
Cash Offer in 24 Hours
  • Idaho Homestead Exemption: inherited, behind on payments, tenants or repairs, we buy the house as-is
  • No fees, commissions or closing costs on a Idaho Homestead Exemption sale
  • Turn the Idaho Homestead Exemption offer down and you owe us nothing

Selling a Idaho House? Get a Cash Offer

We buy as-is.

Call or Text  (424) 435-2326


Last updated November 14, 2026.

What the official sources say

  • The homestead exemption is the first $125,000 of assessed market value of the homestead or 50% of market value, whichever is less. (Idaho Code 63-602G. Homestead; source)
  • An owner need apply only once if the owner still occupies the same homestead; the exemption is not prorated. (Idaho Code 63-602G(4)-(5); source)
  • To receive the exemption for the current tax year, application must be made by the end of business on the last business day of the year; approved applications received after the second Monday in July are granted as tax cancellations. (Idaho Code 63-602G(5); source)
  • Claiming more than one homestead exemption triggers recovery of tax up to 7 years plus a penalty equal to the recovered tax on a first instance. (Idaho Code 63-602G(6); source)
Selling in Idaho?
We buy Idaho houses as-is, with no commission, no repairs and no closing costs to you.
Get My Cash Offer →

What does the Idaho homestead exemption mean?

Idaho uses the word homestead for two different protections, and sellers often mix them up. One is a property tax exemption on an owner-occupied home. The other is a debt protection that shields part of a home's equity from creditors.

The tax exemption lives in Idaho Code 63-602G and is applied by your county assessor. The creditor protection lives in Idaho Code title 55, chapter 10. They have different dollar limits, different rules and different effects when you sell, so this page treats them separately.

ProtectionStatuteAmountWhat it does
Homeowner's (tax) exemption63-602GLesser of $125,000 or 50% of assessed market valueLowers the taxable value of the home
Judicial homestead55-1003 and 55-1008Up to $175,000Protects equity from attachment, execution or forced sale for the owner's debts

How much is the homestead tax exemption, and who qualifies?

The exemption removes the first $125,000 of market value, or 50% of market value if that is less, from property taxation. The Idaho State Tax Commission describes it as 50% of the value of your home and up to one acre of land, with a maximum of $125,000. Its history table shows the maximum was $100,000 in 2019 and 2020, then $125,000 for 2021 through 2025.

To qualify, the home must be owner-occupied and be your primary dwelling place. The statute defines primary dwelling place as the single place where you have your true, fixed and permanent home and to which you intend to return when you are away. Under Idaho Code 63-701, the homestead is the dwelling plus the land around it that is reasonably necessary for use as a home, not more than one acre.

  • You certify to the county assessor that you are applying and that the home is your primary dwelling.
  • You certify that you have not applied in another county or for another homestead in the same county.
  • A home with a multipurpose office still qualifies, but any part used exclusively for something other than the owner's dwelling does not.
  • An owner can also be a beneficiary of a trust, or a partner, member or shareholder of an entity that holds title, if proof is provided as the statute describes.

Applications ask for your full name, date of birth, current address and previous address, plus an Idaho driver's license or ID number. A new Idaho resident who lacks one has 90 days after the initial application to supply it.

When and how do you apply for the Idaho homestead exemption?

You apply once, through the county assessor, and you must apply by the last business day of the year to get the exemption for that tax year. The full exemption takes effect as of January 1 of the tax year in which a complete application is submitted and approved, and it is not prorated.

Approved applications received after the second Monday in July are granted as tax cancellations for the amount of the exemption the property qualified for. A late application is handled differently from one filed before that date.

You do not have to reapply every year as long as you still occupy the same homestead and it is still your primary dwelling. Each county assessor prescribes the form.

What happens to the exemption if you sell, rent out or inherit the home?

The exemption depends on the owner living in the home, so it does not travel with the property automatically. The one-time application only holds while the same owner still occupies the same homestead. A buyer who plans to live in your house should expect to file for the exemption on their own.

Renting the house changes the picture. The statute requires owner occupancy as the primary dwelling, with a specific carve out for owners away on active military service whose homes are leased. Those owners must apply every year by a deadline the county assessor sets, and the county may discontinue the exemption if they miss it.

For an owner who dies, the exemption continues for the year of death and the following tax year as long as the home remains part of the estate. After that, the new owner must reapply and meet the qualification rules. If you are selling an inherited house, this gives the estate a limited window before the tax bill reflects the loss of the exemption. Our Idaho probate guide explains how estates handle the sale itself.

What are the penalties for claiming more than one homestead exemption?

Claiming more than one homestead exemption triggers recovery of tax for up to seven years plus a penalty. The county assessor investigates before granting the exemption and must refuse it if it appears to be improperly claimed. If an improper claim is found later, the assessor decides whether it should have been allowed and, if not, notifies the taxpayer in writing and assesses a recovery.

  • The recovery equals the exempted value times that year's levy, for each year of improper claiming up to seven years, plus costs, late charges and interest.
  • On a first discovered instance of claiming more than one exemption, a penalty equal to the recovered tax is added.
  • A later violation within seven years of that instance is a misdemeanor under the statute.
  • You can appeal the refusal, the recovery or the penalty to the county Board of Equalization within 30 days of the assessor's notice.

Unpaid recovered tax becomes a lien on the real property, and the assessor records a notice of intent to attach a lien 30 days after notifying the taxpayer. If the property is sold to a bona fide purchaser for value before that notice is recorded, the county stops recovering the unpaid amount. If you moved and claimed a new homestead after January 1, the exemption on the old property comes off the following tax year, so tell both assessors when you sell.

How does the judicial homestead protect equity when you sell?

Idaho law exempts the homestead from attachment and from execution or forced sale for the owner's debts, up to $175,000. Idaho Code 55-1003 sets the cap at $175,000 regardless of the lot's area. Section 55-1008 adds that the proceeds of a good faith voluntary sale made to acquire a new homestead, and insurance proceeds held to restore or replace the home, are exempt for one year from receipt, up to the same amount.

That one-year rule is the part sellers should plan around. If you sell the house and intend to buy another, keep the proceeds identifiable and move quickly. The statute says the new homestead acquired with the proceeds is also exempt. If you do not buy a replacement in that year, the protection for the cash may lapse.

Section 55-1008 begins with the words "except as provided in section 55-1005," so the protection has exceptions. We cannot tell you whether your debts fall into one. Talk to an Idaho attorney before closing on a house with judgments or large unsecured debts.

What other Idaho property tax relief affects a home sale?

The homeowner's exemption is the base, and two other programs build on it. The Property Tax Reduction program can reduce taxes by $250 to $1,500 on the home and up to one acre. You must apply every year between January 1 and April 15, and the property must have a current homeowner's exemption. Approved benefits appear on the December property tax bill.

The Property Tax Deferral program lets you postpone paying taxes on the home and up to one acre, but you must pay the taxes and interest later. To qualify for 2027, your 2026 income must be $63,400 or less, and you apply between January 1 and September 7, 2027. If you have deferred taxes and sell, expect the amount owed to come up at closing. The Tax Commission's homeowner page links each program, and the county treasurer can give a payoff figure.

Property taxes are due December 20, with the option of paying half by then and half by June 20. When you sell mid-cycle, ask the county treasurer what has been paid and what is outstanding.

How does a cash sale work if you have a homestead exemption?

A cash sale does not change your exemption rights, but it can shorten the time you carry the home and its tax bill. We buy houses as they are, and we review the property, the title and the county tax status before making an offer. We do not quote prices without seeing the house.

  1. Pull your latest assessment notice and tax bill from the county assessor and treasurer.
  2. Check whether the homeowner's exemption, reduction or deferral is active on the parcel.
  3. List liens, judgments or deferred taxes that must be cleared at closing.
  4. If you plan to buy another home, talk to an attorney about the one-year proceeds rule before you sign.

Nothing here is legal or tax advice. The statutes change, and the legislature updates its online Idaho Code each July after a session, so confirm the current text with the county office or a licensed professional.

More questions about Idaho Homestead Exemption

How much is the Idaho homestead exemption?

The tax exemption is the first $125,000 of assessed market value or 50% of market value, whichever is less. The separate creditor protection under Idaho Code 55-1003 goes up to $175,000.

Do I have to reapply for the Idaho homestead exemption every year?

No, not if you still occupy the same homestead and it remains owner-occupied. You apply once, with the county assessor, and the exemption continues. Owners away on active military service with a leased home must reapply every year.

What is the deadline to apply?

Apply by the end of the county's normal business hours on the last business day of the year to receive the exemption for that tax year. Approved applications received after the second Monday in July are granted as tax cancellations.

What happens to the exemption when a homeowner dies?

It continues for the year of death and the next tax year while the home stays part of the estate. After that, the new owner must reapply and meet the qualifications.

Can I claim homestead exemptions on two homes in Idaho?

No. Claiming more than one triggers recovery of tax for up to seven years and a penalty equal to the recovered tax on a first instance. A later violation within seven years is a misdemeanor.

Are sale proceeds protected after I sell my Idaho home?

Proceeds of a good faith voluntary sale made to acquire a new homestead are exempt for one year from receipt, up to the 55-1003 amount, and so is the new homestead bought with them. Talk to an attorney about your own debts.

title: Idaho Estate and Inheritance Tax: What Heirs Owe When Selling
content:
Idaho Estate and Inheritance Tax: What Heirs Owe When Selling

Cash Home Buyers in Idaho
Cash Offer in 24 Hours
  • Idaho Estate and Inheritance Tax: inherited, behind on payments, tenants or repairs, we buy the house as-is
  • No fees, commissions or closing costs on a Idaho Estate and Inheritance Tax sale
  • Turn the Idaho Estate and Inheritance Tax offer down and you owe us nothing

Selling a Idaho House? Get a Cash Offer

We buy as-is.

Call or Text  (424) 435-2326


Last updated November 14, 2026.

What the official sources say

  • Idaho has no gift tax or inheritance tax, and its estate tax expired in 2004. (Estates and Taxes | Idaho State Tax Commission; source)
  • Idaho estate tax requirements apply only to deaths before Jan. 1, 2005. (Estates and Taxes | Idaho State Tax Commission; source)
Selling in Idaho?
We buy Idaho houses as-is, with no commission, no repairs and no closing costs to you.
Get My Cash Offer →

Does Idaho have an estate tax or an inheritance tax?

No. The Idaho State Tax Commission states that Idaho has no gift tax or inheritance tax, and that its estate tax expired in 2004. The estate tax rules it still describes apply only to deaths before January 1, 2005.

For an heir selling a house in Idaho, that means no state death tax is due on the transfer itself. The Commission's estates and taxes page gives a Boise-area number, (208) 334-7660, and a toll-free number, (800) 972-7660, for questions about deaths before 2005.

Other taxes can still touch an inherited house: federal estate tax for very large estates, income tax on a gain after the sale, and the property tax bill that continues to arrive while the estate is open.

When does the federal estate tax apply?

Federal estate tax is a concern only for estates above the basic exclusion amount, which the IRS lists as $15,000,000 for people who die in 2026. The same figure is the filing threshold for the year of death.

ItemAmount (2026)Source
Basic exclusion amount$15,000,000IRS, What's new, estate and gift tax
Estate tax filing threshold$15,000,000IRS, estate tax
Annual gift exclusion per donee$19,000IRS, What's new, estate and gift tax

Source: IRS, What's new, estate and gift tax. The IRS attributes the 2026 figure to the Working Families Tax Cuts law, so confirm the amount for the year of death.

The threshold applies to the whole estate, not the house alone. Executors add up real estate, accounts, business interests and other assets to see whether a federal return is needed.

How does an heir's basis work when an Idaho house is sold?

An heir generally takes a basis equal to the property's fair market value on the date of the owner's death, according to IRS Publication 551. Gain is measured from that value, not from what the original owner paid decades earlier.

  • If the house sells soon after death at about the date-of-death value, the gain is small.
  • If it is held and the market rises, the gain above the date-of-death value is taxable.
  • If the decedent received the property as a gift within a year before death, a different rule can apply.
  • A written appraisal as of the date of death is useful support for the figure.

If you then sell in Idaho, our Idaho capital gains guide explains the state's 60% deduction for qualifying real property held 12 months. Ask a tax professional how the 12-month holding period is counted for inherited property.

Who can sell an inherited house in Idaho?

The personal representative appointed by the court can sell it. Idaho Code 15-3-711 gives a personal representative the same power over title to estate property that an absolute owner would have, held in trust for the people entitled to it, and the section 15-3-715 list of authorized transactions includes selling, mortgaging or leasing real or personal property of the estate.

The same section allows a personal representative to:

  • dispose of land, in Idaho or another state, for cash or on credit, at public or private sale;
  • make ordinary or extraordinary repairs to buildings;
  • pay taxes, assessments and the costs of administration;
  • hire attorneys, auditors or agents to help.

These powers are subject to limits in the will or in a court order, so a will that restricts sale changes the answer. Idaho Code 15-3-714 also protects a person who deals with a personal representative, since a limiting provision is effective only against those with actual knowledge of it.

What about the small estate affidavit?

Idaho Code 15-3-1201 lets a successor collect certain assets by affidavit when the probate estate is worth $100,000 or less, but its text does not mention real estate. It applies after 30 days have passed since death, and only if no petition for a personal representative is pending or granted anywhere.

The statute names payment of debts, tangible personal property, instruments of debt and securities. A house is therefore not clearly within this shortcut. Ask the title company which documents it needs to close, and speak to a probate attorney if the estate is under the threshold but holds real property.

The affidavit must state that the fair market value of the entire estate subject to probate, less liens and encumbrances, does not exceed $100,000. The Department of Health and Welfare is treated as a successor for medical assistance recovery in some cases, under subsection (c). Our Idaho probate guide explains the court route in full.

Which Idaho statutes govern an estate sale?

Estate administration is in Title 15 of the Idaho Code, the Uniform Probate Code, Chapter 3, which covers probate of wills and administration. The chapter is organized in parts that matter to a house sale.

PartSubject
Part 7Duties and powers of personal representatives
Part 10Closing estates
Part 11Compromise of controversies
Part 12Collection of personal property by affidavit and summary procedure for small estates
Part 13Uniform estate tax apportionment

Source: Idaho Legislature, Title 15, Chapter 3. Part 13 exists to apportion estate tax among recipients, which does not create a state tax.

A lifetime transfer is a different question. Idaho has no gift tax, and the federal annual exclusion is $19,000 per recipient for 2026. A gift of real estate worth more than that amount is a federal question to raise with a tax professional. Our Idaho quitclaim deed guide covers the deed itself.

What costs should an Idaho heir expect while the house is unsold?

The estate remains responsible for property tax, insurance and upkeep from the date of death until closing. County rules are the same as for any owner. In Ada County, for example, the first half is due December 20 and the second half June 20, with a 2% late charge and monthly interest on a late payment.

Section 15-3-715 lets the personal representative pay taxes and administration expenses from estate funds. The homeowner's exemption lasts until ownership changes or the home stops being a primary residence, according to the state, so ask the county Assessor whether it continues after a death.

Our Idaho property tax guide and the county guides for Ada and Canyon list the assessor and treasurer offices.

What do heirs in Idaho commonly face?

An inherited house that sits vacant still generates property tax, utilities and insurance costs, and any will restriction or court order has to be sorted out before a sale.

We buy houses as is in Idaho, including inherited ones, so cleanout and repairs do not need to come first. Call or text for a written cash offer. If you decline it, you owe us nothing. Before accepting any offer, make sure the personal representative has the authority described above and a licensed attorney has reviewed the estate documents.

More questions about Idaho Estate and Inheritance Tax

Does Idaho have an inheritance tax?

No. The Idaho State Tax Commission says Idaho has no gift tax or inheritance tax, and its estate tax expired in 2004.

Do I owe tax when I inherit a house in Idaho?

Idaho does not tax the inheritance itself. You may owe income tax on a gain if you later sell for more than the date-of-death value.

What is the federal estate tax exemption for 2026?

The IRS lists a basic exclusion amount of $15,000,000 for people who die in 2026, and the filing threshold is the same.

Can a personal representative sell real estate without court approval?

Idaho Code 15-3-715 lets a personal representative sell estate real property unless the will or a court order restricts it, so check both.

Is a small estate affidavit enough to sell a house?

Probably not. Idaho Code 15-3-1201 covers payment of debts, tangible personal property, instruments and securities for estates of $100,000 or less, and it does not name real estate.

content:
Idaho Quitclaim Deed: Recording, Fees and When It Works

Cash Home Buyers in Idaho
Cash Offer in 24 Hours

  • No fees, commissions or closing costs on a Idaho Quitclaim Deed sale

Call or Text  (424) 435-2326


Last updated November 14, 2026.

What the official sources say

  • A conveyance of real property must be in a signed writing that states the grantee's name and complete mailing address. (Idaho Code 55-601; source)
  • Recorder fee for deeds and transfers of title of 30 pages or less is $15.00. (Idaho Code 31-3205(1)(b); source)
  • Deeds, grants and transfers of title of 30 pages or less: $15.00; trust deeds or mortgages: $45.00; reconveyances and releases of mortgage: $15.00. (Idaho Code 31-3205(1)(b); source)
  • A conveyance of real property must be in writing signed by the grantor or authorized agent, and the grantee's name and complete mailing address must appear on the instrument. (Idaho Code 55-601; source)
Selling in Idaho?
We buy Idaho houses as-is, with no commission, no repairs and no closing costs to you.
Get My Cash Offer →

What does an Idaho quitclaim deed actually do?

An Idaho quitclaim deed hands over whatever interest the signer has in a property, without promising that the interest is good. A county recorder in Idaho describes a quitclaim as a conveyancing instrument that makes no warranties and simply releases the grantor's current right, title and interest (Bannock County Recorder).

That wording is the key to when it works. The deed moves what the grantor has, and nothing more. If the grantor owns the whole house, the grantee gets the whole house. If the grantor owns half, the grantee gets half. If the grantor owns nothing, the deed passes nothing.

Idaho law treats the conveyance as final between the parties. A grant of an estate in real property is conclusive against the grantor and anyone who later claims under the grantor, with one exception: a purchaser or encumbrancer who acts in good faith, pays value and first duly records an instrument can come out ahead (Idaho Code 55-606). That exception is why recording matters so much, and the later sections come back to it.

When does a quitclaim deed make sense in Idaho?

A quitclaim works best between people who already trust each other and already know the title. It is a poor fit for a sale to a stranger, because the buyer gets no promise about the title.

  • Adding or removing a spouse. A couple who own a home together can change how title is held.
  • Moving a house into a trust or an LLC. The owner and the new holder are effectively the same person or group.
  • Clearing a name from title after a divorce or a family agreement. One person releases whatever claim they have.
  • Fixing a gap. A person who may hold a stray interest signs to release it.

It works less well when the property is being sold on the open market. A buyer using a lender will usually expect a title company to insure the title, and a bare quitclaim leaves the insurer with the job of checking everything behind it. For an heir or co-owner who wants a quick cash sale, the deed is usually one step in a longer title path, not the end of it. If you are unsure whether the person signing actually holds title, find out before the deed is signed, not after it is recorded.

What must an Idaho deed contain to be valid?

An Idaho deed must be in writing, signed by the person giving up the property or an agent authorized in writing, and it must show the grantee's name and complete mailing address (Idaho Code 55-601). The mailing address requirement is easy to miss and is a common reason a recorder questions a document.

Before it can be recorded, the signature must be acknowledged, which in practice means signing before a notary or other authorized officer. The statute lists who acknowledges for different signers: the person executing it, a corporation's officer, a partner, or a manager or member of a limited liability company. A deed signed and acknowledged in another state or country under that place's law is entitled to record, and a certificate of acknowledgment attached to it is prima facie sufficient (Idaho Code 55-805).

If an attorney in fact signs, the power of attorney has to be filed for record in the same office before the deed itself is recorded (Idaho Code 55-806). A quick checklist helps:

  • Grantor's signature, acknowledged
  • Grantee's full name and complete mailing address
  • A legal description of the property that matches the existing record
  • Recorded power of attorney first, if an agent signs

Where and how is an Idaho deed recorded?

A deed is recorded with the county recorder of the county where the property sits (Idaho Code 55-808). An instrument counts as recorded when, being duly acknowledged, it is deposited with the proper officer at the recorder's office (Idaho Code 55-809).

Kootenai County is a useful example of how a local office presents it. The county recorder lists hours of 9 a.m. to 5 p.m. Monday through Friday, excluding holidays, charges the standard $10 for the first page and $3 for each additional page on document types without a special rate, and sells copies of recorded documents at $1.00 per page (Kootenai County Recorder). Other counties publish their own hours and methods, so call or check the county website before sending a deed.

State law also says instruments delivered to a county recorder are recorded rather than merely filed, except plats, surveys, corner records and Uniform Commercial Code instruments (Idaho Code 31-3205(4)).

What do Idaho recorders charge for deeds and related documents?

Idaho sets recording fees by statute, and a deed of 30 pages or less costs $15.00 to record. The table lists the amounts from Idaho Code 31-3205.

ItemStatutory fee
Deeds, grants and transfers of title (30 pages or less)$15.00
Other instruments, first page$10.00
Each additional page$3.00
Reconveyance of a trust deed or release of a mortgage (30 pages or less)$15.00
Power of attorney$25.00
Substitution of trustee$10.00
Copy of a record, each page$1.00
Certificate under seal, when required$1.00
Taking an acknowledgment, including seal$1.00

These are the recorder's fees. A notary, a title company or an attorney may charge separately for their own work. A deed that runs longer than 30 pages falls under the per-page schedule instead of the flat $15.00.

What happens if a quitclaim deed is never recorded?

An unrecorded deed still binds the people who signed it, but it leaves the new owner exposed. Idaho Code 55-815 says an unrecorded instrument is valid between the parties and those who have notice of it, while Idaho Code 55-812 makes an unrecorded conveyance void against a later purchaser or mortgagee in good faith who records first (lease terms of one year or less are treated differently).

Recording flips that risk. Once an acknowledged conveyance is recorded, its filing with the recorder is constructive notice of its contents to everyone (Idaho Code 55-811). Anyone who later checks the county records is treated as having been warned.

For a seller, this has a direct cost. If a family member quitclaimed a share to you and never recorded it, a buyer's title search may not show your ownership. A title company will usually want the gap cured before a closing, and that can slow a sale you wanted to be quick. Record the deed as soon as it is signed and acknowledged.

How does a quitclaim deed affect property tax and a later sale?

A deed changes the name on title, but it does not change what is owed on the parcel. Idaho property tax is due December 20, or in halves with the second half due June 20, and the tax follows the property (Idaho Code 63-903). A new owner who receives a deed from a relative takes the parcel with whatever is unpaid.

The homestead exemption depends on the owner living in the home as a primary dwelling, and the owner certifies to the county assessor that no other homestead exemption is claimed (Idaho Code 63-602G). After a transfer, ask the assessor whether the exemption stays, ends or needs a new application.

When a quitclaim is part of a probate or family transfer and the house will be sold, line up these items first:

  • A title report showing who actually holds title today
  • The recorded deed, with its instrument number
  • A payoff figure for property tax and any loan
  • Written agreement among co-owners if more than one person must sign the sale

More questions about Idaho Quitclaim Deed

Do I need a notary to record an Idaho quitclaim deed?

Yes in nearly every case. Idaho Code 55-805 requires the signer's execution to be acknowledged, or proved and certified, before an instrument can be recorded. A deed acknowledged in another state under that state's law is also entitled to record.

How much does it cost to record a deed in Idaho?

The statutory fee for a deed or transfer of title of 30 pages or less is $15.00. Notary and attorney fees are separate.

Does a quitclaim deed guarantee I own the house?

No. A quitclaim makes no warranties and releases only the grantor's current interest. If the grantor had no title, the grantee receives none.

Where do I record an Idaho deed?

With the county recorder in the county where the property is located. Idaho Code 55-808 places the record in that county.

What must the deed say about the buyer?

It must include the grantee's name and complete mailing address, and it must be in a signed writing, under Idaho Code 55-601.

Idaho Capital Gains Tax When You Sell a House

Cash Home Buyers in Idaho
Cash Offer in 24 Hours
  • Idaho Capital Gains Tax When You Sell a House: inherited, behind on payments, tenants or repairs, we buy the house as-is
  • No fees, commissions or closing costs on a Idaho Capital Gains Tax When You Sell a House sale
  • Turn the Idaho Capital Gains Tax When You Sell a House offer down and you owe us nothing

Selling a Idaho House? Get a Cash Offer

We buy as-is.

Call or Text  (424) 435-2326


Last updated November 14, 2026.

What the official sources say

  • Idaho allows a deduction of 60% of capital gain net income from sale of qualified Idaho property for individual taxpayers. (Idaho Code 63-3022H. Deduction of capital gains; source)
  • Real property qualifies if it has Idaho situs and was held at least 12 months. (Idaho Code 63-3022H(3)(a); source)
  • The deduction is computed on Form CG. (Capital Gains | Idaho State Tax Commission; source)
  • The Idaho income tax rate for 2025 is 5.3% on Idaho taxable income. (Individual Income Tax Basics | Idaho State Tax Commission; source)
Selling in Idaho?
We buy Idaho houses as-is, with no commission, no repairs and no closing costs to you.
Get My Cash Offer →

How does Idaho tax the gain when you sell a house?

Idaho includes a home sale gain in your state taxable income, and it lets you deduct 60% of the gain from qualifying Idaho property. The Idaho State Tax Commission describes a capital gain as what you receive for a capital asset above its cost or other basis. A gain on an asset held one year or less is short term, and a gain on one held longer is long term.

The statute does not set a separate rate. Whatever gain is left after the deduction stays in taxable income, and the Commission lists a single rate of 5.3% on Idaho taxable income for 2025. That rate dropped from 5.69%, effective January 1, 2025, so check the rate for the year you sell.

Federal tax is a separate layer. This page covers the Idaho side, and what Idaho starts from is the gain you report federally.

What does Idaho Code 63-3022H say?

Idaho Code 63-3022H gives an individual a deduction equal to 60% of capital gain net income from the sale or exchange of qualified property, for tax years after 2001. The statute sets the main limits:

  • The property must have had an Idaho situs at the time of sale.
  • Real property must be held at least 12 months.
  • The deduction cannot exceed the capital gain net income from all property included in taxable income.
  • Gains that the Internal Revenue Code treats as ordinary income do not qualify.
  • The deduction is reduced by any federal capital gains deduction for the same property, but not below zero.
  • Property depreciated under section 1245 is not treated as real property for the deduction.

Estates, trusts, S corporations, partnerships and LLCs can also hold qualified property, so the deduction is not limited to people selling a personal residence. Part-year and nonresident owners of multistate entities compute it under State Tax Commission rules.

Which Idaho property sales qualify?

Idaho real property qualifies once you have held it 12 months, for sales on or after January 1, 2005. Sales before that date needed 18 months. For this deduction the Commission defines real property as land, and includes easements, grazing permits and other section 1250 property.

PropertyHolding periodQualifies?
Idaho real property12 monthsYes
Timber grown in Idaho24 monthsYes
Cattle or horses for breeding, draft, dairy or sporting use24 monthsYes
Real property outside IdahoAnyNo
Stocks, bonds, LLC or S corporation interestsAnyNo

Source: Idaho State Tax Commission, capital gains. For an installment sale, the holding-period test is the one in effect in the year of the sale, under Income Tax Administrative Rule 171.06c.

A house you owned for under a year is therefore outside the deduction, which matters to flippers and to anyone who bought, repaired and resold quickly.

How does the federal home sale exclusion interact with Idaho?

The federal exclusion lets you remove up to $250,000 of gain from income, or $500,000 on a joint return, if you owned and lived in the home as your main home for at least two of the last five years. That is IRS guidance in Topic 701 and Publication 523.

Idaho's Form CG then asks for the qualifying gain from sale of a personal residence as it appears on federal Schedule D. The form's wording points to the taxable gain from the sale of your Idaho home, so the Idaho deduction would apply to the gain that remains after the federal exclusion. Confirm that treatment with a tax professional for your sale.

An illustration, ignoring other income and credits: a single owner who has $100,000 of gain left on Schedule D after the exclusion would deduct 60%, or $60,000, on Idaho Form CG. The remaining $40,000 times 5.3% is $2,120 of Idaho tax. This arithmetic shows how the deduction works. It is not a prediction for your return.

What forms and records do you need?

Idaho requires Form CG, Capital Gains Deduction and Instructions, to compute the deduction. The form asks for a description of the property and its Idaho location, the dates acquired and sold, the sales price, cost or other basis and the gain or loss.

  • The settlement statement from the sale, to document the price and selling costs.
  • Records of your purchase price and improvements, to support basis.
  • Federal Schedule D information, since Form CG draws on it.
  • Proof of the dates you bought and sold, to show the 12-month holding period.

The Commission's Form CG page has the current form. Idaho Income Tax Administrative Rules 170 to 173 cover the deduction in general, qualified property, revenue-producing enterprises and pass-through entities.

What about inherited houses and basis?

Inherited property generally takes a basis equal to its fair market value at the date of the decedent's death, according to IRS Publication 551. That can leave little gain on a house the family sells soon after the death.

If the heir sells at close to the date-of-death value, there may be little or no gain to deduct. If the house is held and appreciates before the sale, the gain above the stepped-up value is a normal capital gain, and Idaho's 60% deduction can apply once the holding period is met. Publication 551 notes exceptions, such as property given to the decedent within a year before death. Our Idaho estate and inheritance tax guide covers the death-tax side.

How is the holding period counted?

Idaho borrows the federal holding-period rules in section 1223 of the Internal Revenue Code, with a few state adjustments. Time held by a corporation other than an S corporation does not count, and neither does time held in property you gave up in an exchange if that property would not have qualified.

For a house, the count usually runs from the date you acquired it to the date you sold it. The statute requires at least 12 months, so count carefully from your closing date and confirm the exact day with a tax professional. If an S corporation or an entity taxed as a partnership distributed the property to you, the time that entity held it counts toward your 12 months, whether or not the distribution was a liquidating one.

The statute covers a sale or an exchange, so a swap of real property is analyzed under the same section.

What do Idaho sellers worry about most?

Questions that come up include a house sold within 12 months of purchase, a rental that was never a main home, and an owner who lives in another state. The first is a plain holding-period test. The statute also excludes gains that the Internal Revenue Code treats as ordinary income.

It helps to keep the tax separate from the fees. A capital gain is reported on your income tax return, while closing costs and any back property tax come out of the proceeds at settlement. If the house needs work or carries unpaid taxes, a cash buyer can close without repairs. We buy houses as is in Idaho. Call or text for a written offer, and if you turn it down you owe us nothing.

Whichever route you take, have a licensed tax professional run your numbers before you sign.

More questions about Idaho Capital Gains Tax When You Sell a House

Does Idaho have a capital gains tax?

Idaho taxes capital gains as part of income at its regular rate, 5.3% for 2025, but allows a deduction of 60% of qualifying gain from Idaho real property held at least 12 months.

What form claims the Idaho capital gains deduction?

Form CG, Capital Gains Deduction and Instructions, computes the deduction. It includes a line for the qualifying gain from the sale of a personal residence as shown on federal Schedule D.

Does Idaho follow the $250,000 home sale exclusion?

Idaho starts from the gain reported on federal Schedule D, so gain excluded under the federal rule is not part of what Idaho taxes. Confirm the details of your case with a tax professional.

Do I owe Idaho tax if I sold a house I owned for 10 months?

The 60% deduction requires a 12-month holding period for real property, so a house held 10 months would not qualify for it.

Can an out-of-state owner use the deduction?

The property must have an Idaho situs at the time of sale. For part-year and nonresident owners of multistate entities, the deduction is computed under State Tax Commission rules.

content:
Idaho Probate Process and Selling Inherited Property

Cash Home Buyers in Idaho
Cash Offer in 24 Hours
  • Idaho Probate Process and Selling Inherited Property: inherited, behind on payments, tenants or repairs, we buy the house as-is
  • No fees, commissions or closing costs on a Idaho Probate Process and Selling Inherited Property sale
  • Turn the Idaho Probate Process and Selling Inherited Property offer down and you owe us nothing

Selling a Idaho House? Get a Cash Offer

We buy as-is.

Call or Text  (424) 435-2326


Last updated November 14, 2026.

What the official sources say

  • The small-estate affidavit must state that no application for appointment of a personal representative is pending or granted in any jurisdiction. (Idaho Code 15-3-1201(a)(3); source)
  • Section 15-3-1201 addresses collection of personal property and instruments; it does not by its text transfer real property. (Idaho Code 15-3-1201; source)
  • A transfer from a transferor who has not occupied the property within one year and acquired it by inheritance or devise is exempt from the seller disclosure requirement. (Idaho Code 55-2505(14); source)
Selling in Idaho?
We buy Idaho houses as-is, with no commission, no repairs and no closing costs to you.
Get My Cash Offer →

What is probate in Idaho, and when does a house go through it?

Probate in Idaho is the court process that moves ownership of a dead person's property to the people entitled to it. The Idaho Court Assistance Office publishes a state bar guide that says probate is not a taxation process, and that it is generally necessary in Idaho when title to property must be transferred.

In a probate, a court decides whether a will is valid if there is one, and an inventory is made. Heirs are located, creditors are identified and paid, tax returns are filed, and title is formally transferred. Property that passes by beneficiary designation, such as life insurance proceeds and retirement plans, sits outside the probate estate.

For a house, the practical question is who has legal authority to sign the deed. Until a personal representative is appointed, or another lawful transfer route is completed, an heir usually cannot sell the property alone. That is why many inherited houses sit for months before a sale.

What is the difference between informal and formal probate?

Idaho has adopted the Uniform Probate Code, and the Court Assistance Office guide says that makes probate simpler than in states that have not modernized their codes. The probate can be informal or formal, and either can be supervised or unsupervised by the court.

PathWhat the state bar guide says
Informal probateSometimes the court can handle it without hearings, which may bring speed and simplicity
Formal probateThe court gives full attention, including a ruling on whether a will exists and who the heirs are, with full notice to interested parties
SupervisedCourt direction and protection for the personal representative
UnsupervisedNo court direction or protection for the personal representative
Summary administrationAvailable when a spouse is the beneficiary, with assets passing to the spouse on an expedited basis

The guide recommends formal probate when there are disputes about a will's validity or the appointment of a personal representative, questions about heirs, or challenges to distribution. Its drawbacks are time and cost. A buyer, including a cash buyer, will look at which path your estate is on because it affects when the personal representative can sign.

Can a small estate skip probate in Idaho?

Only for personal property, and only up to a limit. Under Idaho Code 15-3-1201, 30 days after death a person holding the decedent's tangible personal property or owing a debt to the decedent must deliver it to a person claiming to be the successor, once presented with an affidavit. The affidavit must state that the entire probate estate, less liens and encumbrances, does not exceed $100,000.

  • At least 30 days must have passed since the death.
  • No application or petition for appointment of a personal representative or for summary administration may be pending or granted in any jurisdiction.
  • The claiming successor must be entitled to the payment or delivery, including as a trust under a will.

The section speaks of tangible personal property, debts, stock and similar instruments. Its text does not transfer real property, so a house usually needs a different route. The statute also treats the Department of Health and Welfare as a successor for recovering medical assistance, after it mails notice to known heirs, successors and creditors. If the decedent received Medicaid, ask the department how that affects the estate.

What if the surviving spouse is the only heir?

Idaho Code 15-3-1205 offers a summary administration for estates where the surviving spouse is the sole devisee or heir. The spouse, or a person claiming through the spouse, files a verified petition that states the marriage and the death. If the decedent left a will, the original must accompany the petition, and notice of hearing is given under section 15-1-401.

If the court finds that the couple were married and the spouse is the sole heir or devisee, it enters a decree with the same effect as a formal decree approving or determining distribution. The petitioner need not appear in person. The spouse or the attorney may appear by phone with a motion, or submit affidavits before the hearing certifying that notice was given and no objection was received.

There is a catch. A spouse who elects this route assumes and is liable for any indebtedness that could be a claim against the estate, and there is no administration of the estate. The state bar guide lists the spouse's liability for the decedent's debts after the date of death among the disadvantages. Talk to an attorney before choosing it, particularly if the decedent had unpaid medical bills or loans.

Can a personal representative sell the house?

Yes, Idaho law lists selling estate real property among a personal representative's powers. Idaho Code 15-3-715(23) lets a personal representative sell, mortgage or lease any real or personal property of the estate, or any interest in it, for cash, credit, or part cash and part credit, with or without security for unpaid balances.

Several things come together before a closing. The personal representative needs a court appointment. Creditors' claims are handled under 15-3-803, which bars claims against the estate unless they are presented within the time limits it sets.

A cash sale can help an estate that needs to pay debts, taxes and upkeep while the court process runs, because there is no loan approval to wait on. We make an offer only after reviewing the house, and we do not quote a price on this page.

How long do you have to open a probate in Idaho?

Generally three years after the death. Idaho Code 15-3-108 says no informal probate or appointment proceeding, and no formal testacy or appointment proceeding, may be commenced more than three years after the decedent's death, with listed exceptions. It also excludes a few proceedings, such as probating a will already probated at the testator's domicile and appointments in estates with a prior appointment.

The statute has exceptions that can change the answer in an older estate, so do not assume that three years has closed the door or left it open. If a parent died several years ago and the house was never retitled, take the facts to an Idaho attorney soon.

What happens to property tax, the homestead exemption and disclosure on an inherited house?

Three Idaho rules affect an estate holding a house. First, Idaho property taxes are due December 20, and the owner may pay half by December 20 and the balance by June 20.

Second, the homestead exemption continues for the year of the owner's death and the next tax year while the home remains part of the estate. After that, the new owner must reapply and qualify. Our Idaho homestead exemption guide explains the exemption.

Third, Idaho Code 55-2505 exempts some transfers from the seller property condition disclosure requirement. A transfer by a fiduciary administering a decedent's estate and a transfer from a decedent's estate are exempt. So is a transfer from a transferor who has not occupied the property within one year and acquired it by inheritance or devise. The exemption does not stop a buyer from inspecting the house or asking questions.

ItemRule
Property tax due datesDecember 20, with half payable by then and half by June 20
Homestead exemption after deathContinues for year of death and next tax year while the home stays in the estate
Small estate affidavit limit$100,000 probate estate, personal property only
Time to start probateThree years after death, subject to exceptions

How do you sell an inherited house in Idaho step by step?

Start by confirming who has authority, then handle title and tax matters before the closing. The steps below match the statutes cited above.

  1. Find the will and the death certificate, and list the decedent's assets and debts.
  2. Decide whether the estate needs informal or formal probate, or whether a spouse can use summary administration.
  3. Have the court appoint a personal representative if the sale requires one.
  4. Check the county treasurer for unpaid taxes and the assessor for the exemption status.
  5. Gather offers, including cash offers, and review them with your attorney.
  6. Close, record the deed at the county recorder's office, and distribute proceeds as the court or the will directs.

The Court Assistance Office has a statewide help line at 208-746-7541, and the Idaho State Bar runs a lawyer referral service. This page is general information, not legal advice.

More questions about Idaho Probate Process and Selling Inherited Property

Do you need probate to sell a house in Idaho?

Usually yes, unless the house passes outside probate or a spouse uses summary administration. The small estate affidavit in Idaho Code 15-3-1201 covers personal property, not real property, so a house generally needs a personal representative or another lawful transfer.

What is the Idaho small estate limit?

$100,000. Under 15-3-1201, the probate estate less liens and encumbrances must not exceed that amount, and at least 30 days must have passed since the death.

Can a personal representative sell a house in Idaho?

Yes. Idaho Code 15-3-715(23) lets a personal representative sell, mortgage or lease estate real or personal property for cash, credit or part of each.

How long do I have to start probate in Idaho?

Generally within three years after the death under Idaho Code 15-3-108, with listed exceptions. Ask an attorney if the death was several years ago.

What is summary administration for a surviving spouse?

A petition process under 15-3-1205 for estates where the spouse is the sole devisee or heir. A court decree follows, but the spouse becomes liable for the decedent's debts and there is no estate administration.

Does the homestead exemption end when the owner dies?

Not right away. It continues for the year of death and the next tax year while the home remains part of the estate, then the new owner must reapply.

Can a cash buyer purchase an inherited house in Idaho?

Yes, as long as the seller has legal authority to sign. We buy houses as they are, and we review the property and the estate paperwork before making an offer.
